title: 160 Effects of artificial shade and chromium supplementation during mid and late gestation of beef cows under heat stress: offspring performance, physiological responses and immunity at birth
content:
Abstract
The objective of this study is to evaluate the effects of providing artificial shade and chromium (Cr) supplementation during mid and late gestation of fall-calving beef cows on the performance and immunity of their offspring at birth. Seventy-two fall-calving Angus-cross cows were used [body weight (BW) = 566 ± 5.38 kg, body condition score (BCS) = 6.3 ± 0.5] in a 2 × 2 factorial arrangement of treatments: access to shade (shade or no shade) and Cr supplementation (Cr or no Cr). The cows were stratified by initial body weight and body condition score and randomly allocated into 1 to 12 pastures of bermudagrass (3 to 5 ha, 5 or 7 cows per pasture). The treatments were: shade and Cr (SC), no shade and Cr (NSC), shade and no Cr (SNC) and no shade and no Cr (NSNC), day 0 to 150 days before calving. Shade was provided by artificial structures made from black polypropylene fabric, with 4.2 m² of shaded area per animal/pasture. Chromium (Cr propionate; KemTRACE Chromium 0.4%, Kemin Industries) was added to a free choice mineral mix (target intake of ~100 g/day/cow) to provide 0.5 mg Cr/kg of total diet. Calf vigor (1 to 5) was recorded as soon as the calf was seen (1-2 hours after birth). Body weight, rectal temperature and blood were collected between 6 to 12 hours after birth. Blood samples were analyzed for the concentration of GGT, AST, ALT, glucose, albumin, creatinine, urea, total protein in an automated chemistry analyzer (Beckman Coulter AU480). Immunoglobulin G (IgG) concentrations in serum were analyzed using commercial ELISA kits. Globulins were calculated by the difference between total proteins and albumin. Serum urea nitrogen (SUN) was estimated as 46.67% of total serum urea. The data was analyzed using the GLIMMIX procedure of SAS 9.4. Calf sex was included as a covariate in all analyses. Significance was defined as P ≥ 0.05, and trends when 0.05 > P ≤ 0.10. Calves born from shaded cows were heavier (34 vs 29 ± 1.45 kg) and showed greater vigor score compared to those born from cows with no access to shade during mid to late gestation (P < 0.01). No difference of treatments was found for concentrations of glucose, albumin, SUN and GGT (P < 0.05). Calves born from shaded cows showed greater concentrations of ALT and AST (P< 0.05) and tended to have greater concentrations of total proteins, globulins, and IgG (P = 0.10). Dams’ supplementation of Cr reduced calves’ rectal temperature, blood creatinine and AST concentrations at birth (P < 0.05). Removing maternal access to shade during mid and late gestations negatively impacted calf performance at birth and altered physiological responses.
